title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10.

title: WAM is capable in BEHAVIOR-1K: the 2nd-place solution to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
abstract: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.

title: Integration of an ABB YuMi collaborative robot and a CNC doctor-blade coater into an event-driven cyber-physical manufacturing workcell
abstract: Abstract This work presents an event-driven cyber-physical manufacturing workcell that integrates an ABB YuMi collaborative robot with a computer numerical control (CNC) doctor-blade coater for laboratory-scale thin-film processing. Both subsystems retain their local motion-control routines, while Node-RED acts as the supervisory layer and coordinates process progression through high-level commands and reported execution states. Communication is implemented through a hybrid Ethernet/Wi-Fi architecture that links robotic handling, solution dispensing, coating, thermal transfer, and sample unloading within a common workflow. Five consecutive integrated executions were completed without reported interruption. A representative end-to-end YuMi–CNC supervisory handoff delay of approximately 12 ms was observed. A separate 320-exchange Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) ping–response characterization between YuMi and Node-RED gave a median of 6 ms, a mean of 25.87 ms, a 90th percentile of 19 ms, a 95th percentile of 113 ms, and a 99th percentile of 361 ms. The mean active process time per deposition was 91.705 ± 2.247 s ( n = 5); the programmed 180 s thermal-treatment dwell was handled as an overlapped, non-blocking stage and was therefore excluded from this metric. During the five runs, the independently monitored X-axis velocity ranged from 23.978 to 24.005 mm s⁻¹ for a programmed value of 24 mm s⁻¹. A sample-level Digital Process Record was generated for every substrate by associating prescribed conditions, monitored variables, environmental snapshots, and execution outcome with a unique sample identifier. The results provide an initial functional and temporal validation of integrating existing laboratory automation while preserving equipment-specific local control.
summary: Abstract This work presents an event-driven cyber-physical manufacturing workcell that integrates an ABB YuMi collaborative robot with a computer numerical control (CNC) doctor-blade coater for laboratory-scale thin-film processing. Both subsystems retain their local motion-control routines, while Node-RED acts as the supervisory layer and coordinates process progression through high-level commands and reported execution states.

title: ProAct: Harnessing Streaming Motion Generation and Agentic Reasoning for Realtime Embodied Social Interaction
abstract: Real-time embodied social interaction places two equally demanding requirements on an agent: continuously generating fluent multimodal interaction behavior, and proactively reasoning over accumulated dialogue and visual context to decide when to take initiative. These requirements must both be satisfied under a strict latency budget, making them difficult to meet simultaneously. We present ProAct , a dual-system framework that manages these time-critical requirements by integrating a low-latency Behavioral System for streaming multimodal interaction with a slower Cognitive System that performs long-horizon social reasoning and produces high-level proactive intentions. The Cognitive System incorporates an efficient memory mechanism and a user-motivation prediction module to reason over accumulated dialogue and visual context and determine when proactive intervention is appropriate. The Behavioral System further includes an intention-conditioned streaming flow-matching motion generator with a disentangled Control-Net branch, which translates deliberative intentions into continuous nonverbal behavior without disrupting interaction fluency. We deploy ProAct on a physical humanoid robot and validate the framework through comprehensive experiments, including real-world user studies, motion-generation benchmarks, and evaluation on ProActBench , a new, targeted benchmark for evaluating proactive trigger detection and restraint in embodied interaction. Code and ProActBench will be released at https://proactrobot.github.io/.
summary: Real-time embodied social interaction places two equally demanding requirements on an agent: continuously generating fluent multimodal interaction behavior, and proactively reasoning over accumulated dialogue and visual context to decide when to take initiative. These requirements must both be satisfied under a strict latency budget, making them difficult to meet simultaneously.

title: OnlyAct: Extracting Action Representations from Foundation Models for World Models
abstract: Video world models promise general-purpose interactive simulators, but their training is limited by action supervision: action labels are scarce, fragmented across incompatible specifications, and do not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus. A common workaround jointly trains an action encoder to compress consecutive frames into a latent action and a decoder to reconstruct the next frame from the previous frame and that latent, forcing the latent to capture only new information. This has two limitations: learning the action space from scratch can limit generalization to unseen domains, and the bottleneck trades expressiveness for separation, with tighter settings losing nuance and looser ones risking scene leakage under domain shifts. We argue for a different starting point: rather than learning actions from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2), whose embeddings of a frame pair already carry substantial action information after large-scale, diverse video pretraining. The remaining challenge is to extract the action while discarding the scene. We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework that pulls together frame pairs sharing the same motion under a different scene and pushes apart pairs from the same scene with different motion, reshaping the geometry of the pretrained space without imposing a reconstruction bottleneck. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol along three axes (action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality) across robot manipulation, camera navigation, game, and driving benchmarks, most of which are unseen during adaptation. Compared with annotation-free latent-action methods, our representations are substantially more expressive while matching their scene invariance, and they yield world models that transfer demonstrated actions to new scenes more faithfully.

title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
abstract: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.
summary: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem.

title: Model-Free Runtime Measurement of Task-Relevant Information
abstract: Autonomous systems increasingly monitor physical kinematics, environmental states and task completion outcomes. While existing work provides methods to plan information seeking actions and interpret acquired observations, current approaches do not monitor whether the live process of information gathering is functioning properly. Consequently, such systems can remain operationally active without resolving outstanding mission requirements. To address this limitation, we introduce Acquisition-State Telemetry (AST), a model free architecture that evaluates ongoing information acquisition from observable evidence relative to declared task requirements. Specifically, a domain interface maps raw observations into task resolution coordinates and normalized comparative representations, which are processed by a fixed causal monitor. This monitor emits two continuous real time signals that quantify (i) prospective progress across unresolved requirements and (ii) informational friction generated when recurrent evidence yields negligible informational gain. We evaluated a single, unadjusted monitor configuration across eight diverse domains including search and rescue dialogue, spatial grid exploration, hierarchical capability acquisition, continuous robotic manipulation, and probabilistic intent estimation. We show that across these domains the friction channel distinguished unproductive stagnation from purposeful exploration prior to task completion, while remaining muted during post completion activity. Furthermore, in closed loop reinforcement learning experiments under early termination constraints, we demonstrate that penalizing informational friction allowed agents to sustain high mission success, whereas unpenalized policies and baselines with matched operational costs failed to complete required tasks.
summary: Autonomous systems increasingly monitor physical kinematics, environmental states and task completion outcomes. While existing work provides methods to plan information seeking actions and interpret acquired observations, current approaches do not monitor whether the live process of information gathering is functioning properly.

title: Few-Shot Residual Adaptation of Pretrained Latent World Models
abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.
summary: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters.

title: YUV20K: a complexity-driven benchmark and trajectory-aware alignment model for video camouflaged object detection
abstract: Abstract The development of video camouflaged object detection (VCOD) is currently constrained by the scarcity of challenging benchmarks and the lack of robustness of models in the face of erratic motion dynamics. Existing methods frequently encounter challenges related to motion-induced appearance instability and temporal feature misalignment, particularly in complex motion scenarios. To address the issue of data bottleneck, we present YUV20K, a pixel-level annotated, complexity-driven VCOD benchmark. It is composed of 24,295 annotated frames, which are organized into 91 scenes and 47 species. It focuses on challenging scenarios, including large displacement motion, camera motion, and four additional complex-motion scenarios. In terms of methodology, a novel framework is proposed, comprising two key modules: motion feature stabilization (MFS) and trajectory-aware alignment (TAA). The MFS module utilizes frame-agnostic semantic basis primitives to stabilize features, while the TAA module leverages trajectory-guided deformable sampling to ensure precise temporal alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance on existing datasets and establishes a competitive baseline on the challenging YUV20K.
summary: Abstract The development of video camouflaged object detection (VCOD) is currently constrained by the scarcity of challenging benchmarks and the lack of robustness of models in the face of erratic motion dynamics. Existing methods frequently encounter challenges related to motion-induced appearance instability and temporal feature misalignment, particularly in complex motion scenarios.

title: Softness is something you also need! Why compliance helps control: information metrics of a passive walker with compliant ankle
abstract: A great gap in adaptivity, flexibility, and dexterity still exists between intelligent robots, whether they are made of rigid or (partially) compliant components, and their naturally evolved animal and vegetal counterparts. One reason could be of `paradigm' nature. On the one hand, most robots (both rigid and soft) are still designed by following a `Cartesian' approach, with top-down control and a clear mind-body separation. Designing artificial agents on the basis of the principles that we observe in biology is not an easy task. The principles of organization of animals and plants rely on morphological computation and emergence of fit behaviors from loosely coupled networks of embodied agents. Modeling and control require radically new approaches. In this paper we briefly recall and explain some seminal mathematical results linking information metrics and dynamics of the agents, already published years ago; we integrate them with some recent methods developed by us and by the community, we highlight some brief remarks about their relevance and we hint to our current and near future work towards finding concrete and efficient ways for the modeling and control of completely or partially compliant artificial agents and for a better understanding of physical intelligence in nature. We present a technical note summarizing phase-space volume calculations for inverted-pendulum and passive-dynamic walking models, following our proposed framework. Starting from the McGeer compass gait, we introduce knee-ankle compliance, foot-rocker effects, and a Ruina-style compass gait with distributed leg inertia. Standard heel-strike maps are derived and used in the estimation of viable phase-space volumes $W(γ)$, based on a state-dependent Monte-Carlo and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces methods. We show how the methods based on RKHS allow deeper and more subtle analysis.
summary: A great gap in adaptivity, flexibility, and dexterity still exists between intelligent robots, whether they are made of rigid or (partially) compliant components, and their naturally evolved animal and vegetal counterparts. One reason could be of `paradigm' nature.

title: Enabling Robot Learning Through Capable Hardware: Preliminary Studies In Multimodal Tactile Sensing, Bimanual Mobile Manipulation, And Semantic Demonstration Synthesis
abstract: Physical AI is continuing to advance rapidly, but its current capabilities are limited by the underlying hardware and perception stack. Robot learning, in particular, is often bottlenecked by current sensing capabilities, which limit the amount of information available to the learning algorithm and the range of tasks that can be attempted. Most robotics operations are contact-rich, meaning it requires robotic systems to have robust tactile sensing and whole-body perception to understand the state of the world during grasping and object manipulation. In this thesis, I present how there is a need to develop more capable hardware and perception capabilities to enable robot learning in robotic dexterous manipulation and mobile manipulation. To show this, I discuss how DenseTact sensors can be improved to provide more reliable tactile sensing in robotic end effectors, how we can utilize the TidyBot++ mobile manipulator platform to enable bimanual mobile manipulation research and education, and how we can use a single RGB video of a human performing a manipulation task to generate a large set of robot demonstrations for downstream policy learning. DenseTact is an optical tactile sensor that provides high-resolution tactile sensing for robotic manipulation. It’s current capabilities include shape and force sensing. Currently, it has reliability limitations in terms of its manufacturing process, calibration pipeline, and overall hardware design. Additionally, it lacks the ability to sense vibration and temperature, which are important for many manipulation tasks. As a result, I am presenting the current progress to move DenseTact to be more antrhropomorphic, reliable in manufacturing and calibration, and to have multimodal sensing capabilities. The strategy for this is to introduce a new version of the DenseTact Mini sensor, an automated calibration pipeline that builds on TensorTouch, and prototyping hardware and software for localized vibration and distributed temperature sensing modalities co-localized with the existing shape and force channels. MR. CRABS is a holonomic bimanual mobile manipulator that is built on the open-source TidyBot++ base. It includes two Realsense D435 depth cameras, one of which has an active pan-and-tilt mechanism for near-ground perception. It also includes a top LIDAR for long-range perception. It also utilizes two Trossen Robotics Widow-X arms. MR. CRABS is designed both as a research platform for bimanual mobile manipulation and as the next-generation educational platform for Stanford’s ME 326, replacing the LoCoBots used previously. The more capable hardware proved to be essential to allow students to complete the course’s final project, allowing them to better navigate the scene and perform more complex manipulation tasks that cannot be done with the LoCoBots. I present that more teams were able to complete more of the final project, and the projects were more complex than in previous years. Finally, I present Semantics as a Present (SAP), a demonstration-augmentation pipeline that turns a single RGB video of a human performing a manipulation task into an N ×M set of robot demonstrations spanning a family of pre-scanned cousin objects, with no depth sensor, no teleoperation, and no per-object annotation. The method recovers per-frame SE(3) object pose from RGB alone via distilled-DINO and depth-ranking losses, grafts the recovered motion onto each cousin via regionweighted semantic 3D Gaussian splat alignment, and replays the grafted trajectories in IsaacLab to mint demonstrations for any downstream policy (diffusion policy, ACT, π0). SAP shares its vision front end with the first two contributions, illustrating the thesis’s central claim: that perception-grounded, capable hardware is what enables modern robot learning to translate from benchmarks to real, contact-rich, bimanual, semantically rich tasks. It is compared with human demonstrations collected with an Realsense camera and teleoperation, then trained on a VLA benchmark and evaluated on a real robot to show that it can achieve comparable performance to the human demonstrations. We evaluate SAP on seven different tasks.
summary: This thesis explores how advanced hardware and perception stacks can overcome current bottlenecks in robot learning for contact-rich tasks. The author presents improvements to DenseTact sensors, the MR. CRABS bimanual mobile manipulator platform, and a video-based demonstration synthesis pipeline.
method: The author introduces a new DenseTact Mini sensor version, an automated calibration pipeline, and localized vibration and distributed temperature sensing modalities. The MR. CRABS platform is constructed using a TidyBot++ base, depth cameras, a LIDAR, and two robotic arms. The Semantics as a Present (SAP) pipeline uses RGB video to recover object pose, aligns motion across cousin objects using 3D Gaussian splats, and replays trajectories in IsaacLab.
key_finding: The author claims that more capable hardware and perception systems enable robot learning to handle complex, contact-rich, bimanual, and semantically rich tasks. Specifically, the MR. CRABS hardware enabled students to complete more complex final projects compared to previous platforms, and the SAP pipeline achieved comparable performance to human teleoperation demonstrations across seven tasks.

title: Biased Error Attribution in Multi-Agent Human–AI Systems Under Delayed Feedback
abstract: Human decision-making is often influenced by cognitive biases, especially under uncertainty and risk. Prior works have studied biases in single-step decision environments with immediate outcomes or in interaction with a single AI agent. However, less attention has been given to (1) cascaded settings with delayed outcomes, where decision at one step influences future system states and (2) to interaction with multiple AI agents. To study this, we designed a naval battle strategy game where participants interact with two AI advisors. We find asymmetric responses to positive and negative outcomes, with significant changes after negative outcomes. Participants failed to identify the actions responsible for failures and misattributed responsibility across AI agents, leading them to modify decisions steps weakly related to the true cause of poor performance. We refer to this behavior as bias in error attribution. Our findings show how cognitive biases can emerge in human-multi AI teams in cascaded settings.
summary: This paper investigates how cognitive biases manifest when humans interact with multiple AI agents in cascaded decision environments with delayed feedback. The authors designed a naval battle strategy game involving participants and two AI advisors to observe behavioral responses under uncertainty.
method: Designed a naval battle strategy game where human participants interact with two AI advisors in a cascaded setting with delayed outcomes.
key_finding: Participants exhibited asymmetric responses to outcomes, struggled to identify the true causes of failures, and misattributed responsibility across the AI agents.

title: To Bot or not To Bot: Integrating a Social Robot into the Actor’s Rehearsal Process
abstract: Effective theatrical rehearsal is essential for actors’ character development, involving intricate cognitive, emotional, and physical processes. Despite well-established traditional techniques that combine individual practice and partner interactions, rehearsal often requires significant time and resources. Emerging digital and robotic technologies present novel opportunities to enhance rehearsal methods; however, their potential as interactive rehearsal aids remains largely unexplored. This research examines the role of a social robot in supporting actors during pre-rehearsal or solo preparation of two scenes from Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie (1944). Thirty actors with different levels of experience participated in three rehearsal settings: solo practice, rehearsal with a robot playing one character, and rehearsal with the robot alternating between two roles. We evaluated the robot's impact via qualitative responses and self-reports. Thematic analysis indicated that robot-assisted rehearsal improved participants’ experience compared to solo rehearsal, especially among less experienced actors. The robot's role-switching capability offered additional depth appreciated mainly by seasoned performers. These outcomes highlight the promise of social robots as rehearsal tools adapted to the experience of actors.
summary: Effective theatrical rehearsal is essential for actors’ character development, involving intricate cognitive, emotional, and physical processes. Despite well-established traditional techniques that combine individual practice and partner interactions, rehearsal often requires significant time and resources.

title: Transformer architectures scaling laws and in context learning in foundation models
abstract: Transformers have evolved from a sequence-to-sequence architecture for machine translation into a general computational framework underlying large language, vision, speech, multimodal, scientific, and decision-making systems. This critical narrative review synthesizes the field along four connected axes: architectural evolution and attention efficiency; neural scaling laws across parameters, data, compute, and inference-time computation; mechanisms and evaluation debates surrounding in-context learning and emergent reasoning; and the expansion of Transformer systems across modalities and application domains. We move beyond a paper-by-paper chronology by comparing architectural choices under explicit constraints of context length, memory bandwidth, training compute, inference latency, data availability, and task structure. Particular attention is given to sparse and IO-aware attention, multi-query and grouped-query attention, mixture-of-experts routing, multimodal integration, and Transformer–state-space hybrids. We reconcile the Kaplan and Chinchilla scaling formulations with later replication and inference-aware analyses, and distinguish training-time scaling from test-time compute scaling. For in-context learning, we synthesize evidence concerning induction heads, implicit task inference, pre-training data composition, and the debate over metric-dependent emergence. The review also broadens application coverage to speech and audio processing, UAVs and autonomous systems, cybersecurity and intrusion detection, communications and networking, and time-series forecasting, in addition to scientific discovery, software engineering, healthcare, and education. Quantitative comparison tables are restricted to studies reporting results on common datasets and metrics, while explicitly noting differences in training protocols and computational budgets. We conclude that progress is increasingly determined not by parameter count alone, but by joint optimization of architecture, data quality, inference compute, hardware efficiency, and deployment constraints.
summary: This narrative review synthesizes the evolution and application of Transformer architectures across multiple domains and modalities. It examines architectural efficiency, scaling laws, in-context learning mechanisms, and the joint optimization of hardware, data, and compute.
method: Critical narrative review synthesizing existing literature across four connected axes, comparing architectural choices under explicit constraints and restricting quantitative comparisons to studies reporting results on common datasets and metrics.
key_finding: Progress is increasingly determined by the joint optimization of architecture, data quality, inference compute, hardware efficiency, and deployment constraints rather than parameter count alone.

title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.
summary: The authors propose an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy integrating Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition to personalize valence-arousal perception during live interactions. In a study with 66 participants, the continual learning enabled agent achieved higher individual utility and elicited greater participant concession rates compared to the baseline.
method: A counterbalanced within-subject study involving 66 participants negotiating with a humanoid robot, utilizing an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy with an asynchronous architecture that updates the facial expression recognition model in the background and converts differential feedback into utility adjustments.
key_finding: The continual learning enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the baseline, while also yielding higher mean arousal estimates and a broader output range.
limitations: Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions.
why_it_matters: The outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time human-agent negotiation.

title: How Much Should Artificial Intelligence Do Without a Physician? An Autonomy Scale for AI Agents in Solid Organ Transplantation.
abstract: Abstract Background: Artificial intelligence in surgery and transplantation is moving from tools that give a single output toward software agents that retrieve data, plan several steps, use other tools, and take actions. Existing autonomy classifications and device frameworks address physical autonomy and fixed-function outputs well, but they do not specify oversight for systems whose behavior depends on intermediate decisions and tool use. Methods: We developed a governance framework by combining Yang and colleagues’ six-level autonomy scale with an agentic overlay covering tool use, data access, action scope, and persistence. We mapped the framework against current U.S. guidance for AI-enabled devices and the American Medical Association’s 2026 framework for agentic AI. We illustrated its application with four worked examples from solid organ transplantation: donor procurement, machine perfusion, and post-transplant monitoring with cell-free DNA and donor-specific antibodies, assigning each plausible agent function a level and governance tier and identifying the controls that apply. Results: The framework assigns each agent function to one of four governance tiers based on autonomy level, reversibility, and consequence. Tier A (levels 0 to 1) requires accuracy testing and query logging. Tier B (level 2) requires bounded limits, full action logs, and drift monitoring. Tier C (level 3) requires clinician approval of each consequential action, prospective evaluation, and named accountability. Tier D (levels 4 to 5) is not recommended for high-consequence decisions in the current evidence period. In the transplant example, the organ-acceptance decision is assigned to Tier C with clinician decision authority, allocation pairing is excluded from agent action, and a protocol-defined perfusion-time limit is enforced deterministically outside the model. Across the four examples, clinicians approve each consequential action, no viability marker drives acceptance alone, and automatic immunosuppression changes are excluded. Conclusions: Oversight of agents in transplant care should scale with autonomy, reversibility, and consequence rather than with product category. Binding rules should be enforced in deterministic code rather than left to model reasoning. Prospective evaluation is required before any agent in a high-consequence transplant decision advances beyond Tier C.
summary: The authors developed a governance framework for artificial intelligence agents in solid organ transplantation by combining an existing autonomy scale with an agentic overlay. They evaluated the framework against current regulatory and medical guidelines and demonstrated its application using four transplant scenarios.
method: The authors created a governance framework by combining Yang and colleagues' six-level autonomy scale with an agentic overlay covering data access, tool use, action scope, and persistence, and mapped it against U.S. device guidance and AMA 2026 agentic AI frameworks using four solid organ transplantation examples.
key_finding: The framework categorizes agent functions into four governance tiers based on consequence, reversibility, and autonomy level, concluding that high-consequence transplant decisions require clinician approval and that binding rules must be enforced deterministically outside the model.

why_it_matters: It provides a structured approach for scaling the oversight of artificial intelligence agents in transplant care according to autonomy, reversibility, and consequence rather than product category.

title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains.

title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.
summary: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences.

title: TanCRAFT: Context-Reasoned Anticipatory Feedback for Assembly Tasks
abstract: Preventing human error in physical assembly tasks requires assistance systems that can intervene before mistakes are made. This is especially challenging in settings where users are free to choose the construction order and correctness depends on the evolving assembly rather than a fixed next step. We present TanCRAFT, a four-stage real-time predictive assistance system that tracks the scene state, reasons about the current partial assembly, forecasts the near-future motion of manipulated pieces, and intervenes when the predicted placement is incompatible with the target. We instantiate our framework and confirm its effectiveness in a controlled tangram assembly task through offline benchmarks and a within-subject user study. Our findings show that the predictive feedback significantly reduces mistakes relative to unguided and reactive sessions, while yielding the lowest mean perceived workload and shortest mean completion time. Overall, these results demonstrate the value of predictive feedback for error prevention and provide a step toward cost-aware assistance for automation and human-robot workcells.
summary: Preventing human error in physical assembly tasks requires assistance systems that can intervene before mistakes are made. This is especially challenging in settings where users are free to choose the construction order and correctness depends on the evolving assembly rather than a fixed next step.

title: Optimization-Based Path Planning for Industrial Manipulators: Experimental Validation in Additive Manufacturing
abstract: Robotic additive manufacturing requires joint paths that reconcile robot feasibility with process-specific geometry. We develop an offline optimization-based path planner that combines joint-path regularity and self-collision penalties with process costs and constraints, so that a new process enters through its own reference, residuals, and tolerances. Full-path and boundary-coupled chunked optimization handle references of different lengths. Iterative Weight Tuning (IWT) determines the cost weights from the gaps between Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and their targets. In carbon-fiber winding and robotic 3D printing, the planned paths meet the geometric tolerances and all KPI targets, and both paths are executed on a UR10e, without extrusion for printing, with joint-level tracking recorded during execution.
summary: Robotic additive manufacturing requires joint paths that reconcile robot feasibility with process-specific geometry. We develop an offline optimization-based path planner that combines joint-path regularity and self-collision penalties with process costs and constraints, so that a new process enters through its own reference, residuals, and tolerances.

title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery
abstract: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.
summary: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters.

title: Game-Enhanced Embodied Learning with Event and Foresight Pretraining
abstract: Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model. Coverage-preserving anchor selection constructs one-second targets, and an attention mask prevents teacher-forced future actions from entering foresight queries. The selected corpus contains 394 recordings across 20 games, with 223.36 hours of recorded timestamp span and 2,072,084 training anchors. After 12,400 game-pretraining updates, we compare the resulting initialization with the public base under the same suite-specific robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success increases from 1,718/2,000 (85.90%) to 1,811/2,000 (90.55%), a gain of 4.65 percentage points. Suite gains are 9.2, 6.8, 0.2, and 2.4 points on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. The 40-task breakdown shows 24 improvements, 10 declines, and six ties. These results support the practical value of the complete game-pretraining stage in this evaluated setting, while revealing heterogeneous task outcomes. The comparison includes additional optimization and does not isolate the effects of game data, the two objectives, or training variability.
summary: Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model.

title: Camera equalisation of an 11.5x drop in environmental illuminance: four imitation-learning policies on an SO-101 arm
abstract: Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated. Four imitation-learning policies (ACT, SmolVLA, Diffusion Policy and pi0.5) were trained on the same 50 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. Each was run for ten rollouts at about 520 lux and again at about 45 lux, an 11.5x reduction. Success was 20/40 in normal light and 19/40 in low light: a change of -2.5 percentage points (95% CI -23 to +19), with no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity (interaction p = 0.86). The recorded video shows why: mean image brightness was only 3% lower in low light on the front camera and 19% lower on the wrist camera. Both cameras were set to automatic exposure and white balance, which most likely absorbed the difference; exposure was not locked in this experiment. An accidental repeat of one 10-rollout block reproduced its success count (7/10) but matched the first block at only 6 of 10 placements, consistent with chance. We conclude that lux alone does not describe what a policy sees. Camera settings, and image statistics compared with the training recordings, are the quantities to report and control. Data and code are public.
summary: Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated.

title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
abstract: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.
summary: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing.

title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

title: Toward Resilient Explainable AI–Digital Twin Frameworks for Cyber-Secure Renewable Energy Systems: An Uncertainty-Aware Lifecycle-Integrated Architecture
abstract: Abstract The accelerating penetration of variable renewable energy sources into modern power systems demands digital infrastructures capable of supporting predictive, autonomous, and trustworthy grid operation. While digital twins (DT) and artificial intelligence (AI)—particularly multi-agent and agentic architectures—are key enablers, their integration remains fragmented across three critical dimensions: explainability, cybersecurity, and uncertainty management. This paper proposes a conceptual, uncertainty-aware, lifecycle-integrated architecture that couples explainable AI (XAI) with digital twin modeling to support resilient, cyber-secure renewable energy operations. Based on a structured review spanning component-, building-, and urban-scale DT infrastructure, XAI-driven forecasting and fault diagnosis, distributed energy resource (DER) multi-agent control, and DER cybersecurity vulnerabilities, we identify a persistent scholarly disjunction. Few studies treat interpretability, adversarial resilience, and stochastic uncertainty as co-design requirements across the entire asset lifecycle. Using a design-science methodology and thematic synthesis, we develop a five-layer architecture: sensing and data acquisition, digital twin simulation, XAI-mediated agentic decision-making, cybersecurity and resilience, and lifecycle governance. The core contribution lies in defining the structural logic through which these layers interoperate to achieve transparency, security, and adaptability. This framework provides a foundation for future simulation-based validation and advances debates on digitalized energy infrastructure governance.

Detailed description of the proposed research Proposed title: Strengthening Industry–Academia Collaboration Through Research and Innovation: Integrating Advanced Technologies, Skill Development, and Industrial Applications for Sustainable Economic Growth. This research investigates the importance of establishing effective partnerships between academic institutions, industrial organizations, and research laboratories to accelerate scientific innovation and industrial development. Academic institutions are important centres for fundamental research, scientific discovery, technical education, and human-resource development. Industries provide practical engineering challenges, manufacturing requirements, technological resources, and opportunities for commercialization. However, differences in research priorities, limited communication, inadequate funding, infrastructure limitations, and intellectual property concerns often restrict the conversion of academic research into practical industrial applications. The proposed study develops an integrated framework to strengthen the connection between academic research and industrial requirements. The research focuses on the following major areas: A. Industry–academia research integration Identification of industrial problems requiring scientific investigation. Joint research projects between universities and industries. Industry-sponsored research programmes. Collaborative laboratories and research centres. Faculty–industry interaction and knowledge exchange. B. Sustainable industrial development Energy-efficient manufacturing. Waste reduction and recycling. Sustainable materials development. Resource optimization. title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_θ(x)\propto\exp(-E_θ(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.

title: CURRENT: A Recurrent Neural Network for Concurrent Spatial and Temporal Super-Resolution of 4D Flow MRI
abstract: Objective: To improve the spatial and temporal resolution of aortic 4D flow MRI through a unified deep learning framework for post-acquisition super-resolution (SR) of reconstructed velocity vector fields. Methods: We propose CURRENT, a recurrent neural network that performs spatial and temporal SR with a single network architecture. Supervised training was conducted using paired low- and high-resolution datasets generated by embedding computational fluid dynamics simulations of aortic flow into in vivo thoracic MRI backgrounds, followed by controlled spatial and temporal downsampling. CURRENT was evaluated for two-fold spatial and temporal SR against 4DFlowNet and for two-fold spatiotemporal SR against sequential spatial and temporal SR pipelines based on 4DFlowNet. Image-based and k-space-based quantitative metrics were considered and conventional interpolation were used as baselines. In addition, the impact of CURRENT's spatiotemporal SR on physics-informed relative pressure estimation was assessed. Finally, the ability of CURRENT to generalize from synthetic training data to in vivo acquisitions was investigated. Results: CURRENT achieved superior spatial SR performance and comparable temporal SR performance to dedicated 4DFlowNet models while providing a unified solution for both tasks. Simultaneous spatiotemporal SR using CURRENT yielded more accurate relative pressure estimates than either spatial or temporal SR alone and outperformed sequential 4DFlowNet-based spatial and temporal SR approaches. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrated promising generalization to in vivo 4D flow MRI data despite being trained exclusively on synthetic datasets. Conclusion: CURRENT provides a unified framework for spatial and temporal SR of 4D flow MRI. The proposed approach has the potential to enhance physics-based analysis and broaden the applicability of accelerated 4D flow MRI.
summary: Objective: To improve the spatial and temporal resolution of aortic 4D flow MRI through a unified deep learning framework for post-acquisition super-resolution (SR) of reconstructed velocity vector fields. Methods: We propose CURRENT, a recurrent neural network that performs spatial and temporal SR with a single network architecture.

title: Interleaving anatomical inspection and diagnostic reasoning for explainable radiology report generation
abstract: Automated radiology report generation can draft clinically plausible reports, yet the pathway from visual evidence to reported findings remains opaque, leaving the diagnostic basis of these reports unexplained and the generated reports difficult to review or revise. We introduce ARIVE (Anatomy-guided Reasoning with Interleaved Visual Evidence), an explainable report generation framework that interleaves anatomical inspection with diagnostic reasoning prior to final report composition. To support this process, we constructed 159,416 multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) trajectories from MIMIC-CXR, wherein visual evidence from inspected anatomical regions informs subsequent clinical interpretation. Trained on these trajectories and further optimized using anatomical and clinical-content rewards, ARIVE achieved superior clinical-efficacy performance compared with strong baselines on MIMIC-CXR and the abnormality-centered MIMIC-ABN. ARIVE's reports were competitive with those of leading models in blinded expert grading, and its MCoT trajectories earned high ratings for diagnostic traceability. Furthermore, a paired review evaluation suggests that access to MCoT can aid in identifying errors within generated reports.

title: Persistent Metric-Semantic Maritime Scene Memory from Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graphs
abstract: Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide robots with persistent metric-semantic representations for spatial reasoning, but the existing methods have primarily been developed for indoor and terrestrial environments. In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed. Our experiments show that zero-shot representative outdoor 3DSG descriptions agree with our labeled ground truth for a majority of geometry-supported objects on our data, but the resulting map exhibits considerable physical-entity fragmentation, and its terrestrial higher-level assumptions don't capture maritime spatial organization needs. We therefore keep the underlying mapping method and post-process its accumulated evidence. We show a metric-semantic consolidation method followed by geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning that reconciles remaining fragments into physical entities and groups entities through observations into local places. In parallel, we construct maritime macro regions using map priors and onboard water and structure observations, and associate them with the local places. The resulting representation reduces physical-entity fragmentation beyond both the baseline and our geometry-semantic consolidation component alone, supports correspondence of fixed local places across repeated maritime traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on our reviewed queries over tested baselines. These results show how an outdoor open-vocabulary map can be adapted into persistent maritime scene memory with our methods for object/place identity and spatial abstractions.

In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed.

title: Industry 4.0 in Bahrain: policy architecture, implementation mechanisms, and manufacturing readiness challenges
abstract: Industry 4.0, or the Fourth Industrial Revolution, denotes the integration of cyber-physical systems, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, big-data analytics, additive manufacturing, and advanced robotics into manufacturing and industrial processes. For small, hydrocarbon-reliant economies such as the Kingdom of Bahrain, the adoption of these technologies is closely linked to economic diversification, fiscal sustainability, and private-sector employment objectives. This study adopted a qualitative policy-analysis design based on desk research and structured document review, supported by a limited comparative benchmarking exercise across selected Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states. The analysis drew primarily on official Bahraini policy materials, including the Ministry of Industry and Commerce (MoIC), the Industrial Sector Strategy 2022–2026, the iFactories national initiative, the Smart Industry Readiness Index (SIRI), Tamkeen, and the Bahrain Economic Development Board (EDB), and triangulated these materials with selected academic and institutional sources. The paper examined how Bahrain’s Industry 4.0 policy architecture was structured, which institutions and instruments supported implementation, how the approach compared with selected GCC initiatives, and which constraints affected implementation, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) manufacturers. The analysis found that Bahrain had developed an institutionally coherent policy framework anchored in iFactories and SIRI-based factory-readiness assessment, but publicly available evidence on implementation outcomes, including productivity, exports, employment, and environmental performance among participating factories, remained limited. Accordingly, the study distinguished between policy design, policy targets, expected benefits, illustrative examples, and verified outcomes, and treated sustainability as a policy linkage rather than a measured outcome. The principal contribution was a structured policy analysis of Bahrain’s manufacturing-readiness agenda and identification of the evidence gaps that future empirical evaluation should address. Analytically, the study was guided by a framework combining industrial-policy theory, absorptive-capacity theory, and Industry 4.0 readiness-assessment approaches, operationalised through seven analytical categories: policy architecture, implementation mechanisms, readiness assessment, financing and support instruments, SME absorptive capacity, sustainability linkage, and monitoring and evaluation.

title: BCAT: A Block Causal Transformer for PDE Foundation Models for Fluid Dynamics
abstract: Background: Foundation models have demonstrated remarkable generalization in vision and language, but their accurate use for scientific computing remains challenging. For two-dimensional fluid-dynamics prediction, current transformer-based models are often hindered by limited context and rigid causality information, as they typically map fixed windows to the next step. Objectives: We aim to develop a unified architecture for heterogeneous fluid-dynamics families. The goal is to better capture the complex spatio-temporal dependencies inherent in nonlinear fluid dynamics. Methods: We introduce BCAT, a block-causal transformer for autoregressive prediction of two-dimensional fluid-dynamics solutions. Our approach adapts block-causal attention to next-frame prediction, leveraging previous frames as contextual priors. The model is trained on 69K trajectory sequences from PDEBench, PDEArena, and CFDBench using the Muon optimizer. Results: BCAT achieved an average relative 𝐿 2 error of 1.18% across the six evaluated fluid families, reducing error by 45% relative to a 3.4-times-larger baseline. In ablations, next-frame prediction was 3.5x more accurate than the corresponding nexttoken variant. A five-seed analysis, noisy-input stress test, long-rollout analysis, and physics diagnostics further characterize the model. Conclusions: The block-causal framework captures spatial interactions within frames while enforcing temporal causality across frames. BCAT provides an accurate and computationally efficient model for the two-dimensional fluid-dynamics benchmarks considered here.
summary: Background: Foundation models have demonstrated remarkable generalization in vision and language, but their accurate use for scientific computing remains challenging. For two-dimensional fluid-dynamics prediction, current transformer-based models are often hindered by limited context and rigid causality information, as they typically map fixed windows to the next step.

title: Exploring the Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Learning Effectiveness Through Motivations
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is an important learning tool in academia and practice for the development of contemporary science and technology. However, few studies have investigated the effect of GenAI on perceived learning effectiveness (LE) through intrinsic psychological states and extrinsic technological features concerning motivation. This study developed and validated an integrated framework based on flow theory (Flow), acting as an intrinsic motivation with its antecedents, interactivity (INT), and challenges (CHA), and the technology acceptance model (TAM), acting as an extrinsic motivation. Data collected from 112 respondents in Macau were tested against the research model using the partial least squares approach. The results indicate that INT and CHA positively influence flow (Flow), which, in turn, promotes LE and attitudes (ATT) toward GenAI. Furthermore, perceived ease of use (PEU) plays a critical role in determining perceived usefulness, which affects subsequent ATT and, ultimately, LE, although PEU does not have a significant effect on ATT. The findings reveal that joint intrinsic and extrinsic motivation could significantly improve learners’ LE in a GenAI-using environment.
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is an important learning tool in academia and practice for the development of contemporary science and technology. However, few studies have investigated the effect of GenAI on perceived learning effectiveness (LE) through intrinsic psychological states and extrinsic technological features concerning motivation.

title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.
summary: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites.

title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model
abstract: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.
summary: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity.

title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters
abstract: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply. We present Earlybird, a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer (16.8 MB at 4 bits). Earlybird learns from audio cut off at random points, including partway through a word, and is asked to predict every word that is due by then in full, plus a guess of the next two words. Its raw token probabilities give a confidence for every word including the one still being spoken. On clean audiobook speech (LibriSpeech test-clean), the median word is predicted correctly 90 ms before the speaker finishes it, while released streaming models get it 90 to 400 ms after it ends. Earlybird is the earliest on all six test sets we time, covering audiobooks, TED talks, public speech, earnings calls, and synthetic speech. On the same audiobooks, 69% of words are predicted correctly before they end, against 3-25% for the other models. For words still being spoken, confidence is calibrated, with an expected calibration error (ECE) of 3.7 to 5.5. On the eight English Open ASR Leaderboard sets, it is more accurate than Moonshine Tiny on every set and roughly ties Whistle, a model of the same size.
summary: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Offline Reinforcement Learning with Online Action Selection Enabled by Sparse Gaussian-Process Critics
abstract: Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data. In its original implementation, the online objective combines the predicted return from a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. We examine the effect of this penalty and replace the critic and AAE with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic. Actions maximise $μ- κσ$, an uncertainty-adjusted estimate of the return from one action followed by the historical operating practice. On the HOFLON polymerisation-reactor benchmark, removing the AAE from HOFLON led to 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs over five critics. At its published weight, the variation in the AAE penalty is four orders of magnitude smaller than the variation in the tree-ensemble critic. Nevertheless, it changes actions when the predicted returns of competing candidates are nearly equal, and paired runs with and without the penalty diverged from the first move. With a Matérn-5/2 sGP critic, $κ= 0$ led to failure in 13 of 15 runs, whereas with $κ= 3$ none of 15 runs (five critics, three noise realisations) failed. The median and lowest returns were 13,464 and 13,398 (HOFLON: 13,393 and 12,411). A squared-exponential sGP critic with learned inducing inputs needed $κ\geq 3$ to remain within the empirical data support in steady state, and then settled with a temperature offset of 2.0 K.
summary: Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data.
