title: SpaRRTa: A Synthetic Benchmark for Evaluating Spatial Intelligence in Visual Foundation Models
abstract: Abstract Visual Foundation Models (VFMs), such as DINO and CLIP, excel in semantic understanding of images but exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities, which limits their applicability to embodied systems. As a result, recent work has incorporated some 3D tasks (such as depth estimation) into VFM training. However, VFM performance remains inconsistent across other spatial tasks, raising the question of whether these models truly possess spatial awareness or overfit to specific 3D objectives. To address this question, we introduce the Spatial Relation Recognition Task (SpaRRTa) benchmark, which evaluates the ability of VFMs to identify static directional relations between visible objects. Unlike traditional 3D objectives that focus on precise metric prediction (e.g., surface normal estimation), SpaRRTa probes a fundamental capability underpinning more advanced forms of human-like spatial understanding. SpaRRTa generates an arbitrary number of photorealistic images with diverse scenes and fully controllable object arrangements, along with freely accessible spatial annotations. Evaluating a range of state-of-the-art VFMs, we reveal significant disparities in their ability to encode directional spatial relations. Through our analysis, we provide insights into the mechanisms that support or hinder this form of spatial awareness in modern VFMs. We hope that SpaRRTa will serve as a useful tool for guiding the development of future spatially aware visual models. Our project page can be found at https://sparrta.gmum.net/ .

As a result, recent work has incorporated some 3D tasks (such as depth estimation) into VFM training.

title: Benchmarking robots for everyday environments: from lab experiments to real-world operations
abstract: This study presents an interdisciplinary process for benchmarking service robots in public everyday environments, addressing the gap between laboratory metrics and real-world operation at technology readiness levels 6–7. Three robots were evaluated in three use cases: outdoor park cleaning, pedestrian underpass cleaning, and interactive assistance in a public library. Over three years (2023–2025), seven benchmarking events (a consensus workshop and six on-site evaluations, two per use case) assessed the robots in increasingly realistic settings, from controlled conditions to public operation. An interdisciplinary panel of experts in robotics, human–robot interaction, safety, and economic viability consolidated use-case-specific metrics into a shared evaluation concept refined across three phases. Rather than ranking the robots, the evaluation examined how task fulfillment, interaction quality, safety, and economic viability interact in the transition from laboratory prototype to operational system. Direct quantitative comparability across the heterogeneous use cases remained limited, characteristic of benchmarking at this maturity level. The process yielded cross-case insights: increasing environmental realism introduces challenges that uniform metrics capture only in part; the interaction-quality guideline works best as a modular instrument adapted to each use case; safety was assessed by occupational-safety and product-certification experts who adapted industrial test procedures for public settings; and economic viability proved a cross-cutting dimension. We conclude that benchmarking at higher technology readiness levels is well served by a shared procedure for selecting and documenting metrics across these four categories, with safety as mandatory, rather than by a fixed set of metrics: generalizability lies in the procedure rather than in identical metrics.
summary: This study presents an interdisciplinary process for benchmarking service robots in public everyday environments, addressing the gap between laboratory metrics and real-world operation at technology readiness levels 6–7. Three robots were evaluated in three use cases: outdoor park cleaning, pedestrian underpass cleaning, and interactive assistance in a public library.

title: Rhythmic-Semantic Co-Speech Gestures for Emotional Dialogue in Robots
abstract: Most data-driven robot systems generate either rhythmic beat-like motion or semantically meaningful iconic gestures, but not both. We present an emotion-aware rhythmic–semantic co-speech gesture system that generates iconic and beat behaviors in real time from text and the robot’s internal emotional state. We propose lightweight models that predict iconic timing and intensity, then fill the remaining spans with emotion-conditioned beats. We train on BEAT2 and deploy on the social robot Haru. In an online user study (N = 60), our method shows stronger speech–gesture alignment and is preferred over baselines.

We present an emotion-aware rhythmic–semantic co-speech gesture system that generates iconic and beat behaviors in real time from text and the robot’s internal emotional state.

title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
abstract: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors.

title: ElasticDino: Dense Semantic Features Using Elastic Deformations
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) serve as the backbone for countless vision tasks, including dense prediction tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, even though the quadratic complexity of self-attention severely limits feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts. In this work, we introduce ElasticDino, a lightweight adapter which produces high-resolution feature maps, adhering to the fine details of the input image. As a key insight, we observe the consistency of artifacts across channels, and simultaneously resolve them to match the input image structure. Using a slim architecture based on spatial deformations, ElasticDino produces pixel-aligned, high-resolution feature maps efficiently. Leveraging deformations allows strictly preserving sharp semantics, and thereby avoiding the smoothness biases inherent to alternative approaches. Due to the absence of ground truth, we employ pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads to predict a set of downstream dense tasks, guiding the deformation process without leaking task-specific semantics into the model. We demonstrate superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance.

title: Digital twins for intelligent intersections: A literature review
abstract: Intelligent intersections play a pivotal role in urban mobility, demanding innovative solutions such as digital twins to enhance safety and efficiency. This literature review investigates the integration and application of digital twins for intelligent intersections, a critical area within smart urban traffic systems. The review systematically categorizes existing research into five key thematic areas: (i) Digital Twin Architectures and Frameworks; (ii) Data Processing and Simulation Techniques; (iii) Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Adaptive Traffic Control; (iv) Safety and Protection of Vulnerable Road Users; and (v) Scaling from Localized Intersections to Citywide Traffic Networks. Each theme is explored comprehensively, highlighting significant advancements, current challenges, and critical insights. The findings reveal that multi-layered digital twin architectures incorporating real-time data fusion and AI-driven decision-making enhances traffic efficiency and safety. Advanced simulation techniques combined with sophisticated AI/ML algorithms demonstrate notable improvements in real-time responsiveness and predictive accuracy for traffic management. Additionally, the integration of digital twins has shown substantial promise in safeguarding vulnerable road users through proactive and adaptive safety strategies. Despite these advancements, key challenges persist, including interoperability of diverse data sources, scalability of digital twins for extensive traffic networks, and managing uncertainty within dynamic urban environments. Addressing these challenges will be essential for the future development and deployment of intelligent, adaptive, and sustainable intersection management systems.
summary: Intelligent intersections play a pivotal role in urban mobility, demanding innovative solutions such as digital twins to enhance safety and efficiency. This literature review investigates the integration and application of digital twins for intelligent intersections, a critical area within smart urban traffic systems.

title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
abstract: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.
summary: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures.

title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
abstract: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.

title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
summary: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA.

title: From Foundation VLM to Versatile Driving VLM: A Triplet Incremental Training Approach
abstract: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.

title: Objectives as Policies: Vision-Language Model Cost Programs for Contact-Rich Manipulation
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong semantic and spatial reasoning capabilities in 3D environments. Recently, connecting VLMs with model-predictive controllers (MPC) has emerged as a paradigm for combining strong semantic reasoning with physics-based planning. However, connecting these two for contact-rich robotic manipulation requires a task representation that bridges the two and captures how physical interactions can be reasoned by VLMs. In this work, we introduce Objectives as Policies (OaP), a framework that connects a pretrained VLM to a shared sampling-based MPC through an editable objective program. Each program specifies a sequence of stages for completing a task, combining running and terminal costs from a cost library with stage completion conditions. Given a natural-language task instruction and scene observation, we build a simulation-based digital twin through real-to-sim, and the VLM generates an objective program that is executed by the MPC in the simulation. The program is iteratively updated by the VLM based on MPC rollouts, before being deployed in the real world. We evaluate our framework in both simulation and the real world on four tabletop manipulation tasks, and show that it outperforms strong baselines. Additional videos and examples are available on the project website: https://zihaolu001.github.io/oap-project/
summary: The authors propose Objectives as Policies, a framework that integrates pretrained vision-language models with model-predictive controllers for contact-rich robotic manipulation tasks. The approach utilizes editable objective programs generated by the vision-language model and executed via simulation-based planning before real-world deployment.
method: The authors introduce a framework where a pretrained vision-language model generates an editable objective program comprising sequential task stages, combining cost functions and completion conditions. This program is executed through a shared sampling-based model-predictive controller using a simulation-based digital twin, and is iteratively updated based on rollouts prior to real-world deployment.

title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($π_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

title: When Will You Hand It Over? A Hidden Start Delay Makes Self-Play Handover Robust to Unfamiliar Partners
abstract: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.
summary: The authors demonstrate that standard cooperative self-play handover policies fail when interacting with unfamiliar partners due to rigid timing expectations. To address this, they introduce hidden start-delay randomisation, which improves generalization to unseen partners without requiring partner retraining.
method: Alternating PPO self-play in a physics-based parcel handover task between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, paired interventions, and hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD).
key_finding: Standard self-play handovers drop significantly in success rate with unfamiliar partners, but adding hidden start-delay randomisation raises success with unseen scripted partners from 31% to 80% while reducing high-force contact.

title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
summary: The authors introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework designed for long-horizon tasks across complex 2D and 3D interactive environments. The system combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning within an end-to-end architecture supported by a cloud-edge inference engine.
method: Continued pre-training on tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction trajectories, followed by sparse-thinking instruction tuning and a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method.

title: FlexMARL: Graph-Driven Rollout-Training Co-Design for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Despite algorithm-level innovations for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the underlying infrastructure for large-scale MARL remains underexplored. Existing training frameworks primarily optimize for single-agent scenarios and fail to capture the graph-structured nature of MARL. This fundamental mismatch leads to three MARL-specific challenges: topology-induced rollout skew, critical path synchronization barriers, and dynamic training demand. To bridge this gap, we propose FlexMARL, a graph-driven rollout-training co-designed framework for large-scale LLM-based MARL. FlexMARL introduces the multi-agent execution graph (MEG) and materializes the intermediate representation as the MEG Store, which provides decentralized multi-table storage and serves as the data hub for system components. Built around the MEG Store, the Rollout Engine develops dependency parallel sampling with hierarchical load balancing, which reduces inference latency and balances intra-agent/inter-agent loads. The Joint Orchestrator exploits an agent-level asynchronous pipeline to mitigate the critical path synchronization barriers while maintaining consistency. The Training Engine achieves on-demand resource allocation by collectively managing training processes for individual agents. The training states of different agents are swapped via location-agnostic communication APIs. Empirical results on a production cluster demonstrate that FlexMARL achieves up to 7.3x speedup and improves hardware utilization by up to 5.6x compared to existing frameworks.
summary: The authors introduce FlexMARL, a graph-driven framework designed to co-design rollout and training for large-scale multi-agent reinforcement learning using large language models. The system addresses infrastructure limitations such as topology-induced rollout skew, synchronization barriers, and dynamic training demands through a centralized data hub and specialized execution engines.
method: The framework utilizes a multi-agent execution graph and a decentralized intermediate storage called the MEG Store, alongside a Rollout Engine for dependency parallel sampling, a Joint Orchestrator for asynchronous pipelining, and a Training Engine for on-demand resource allocation and location-agnostic state swapping.
key_finding: Empirical evaluations on a production cluster demonstrate that FlexMARL achieves up to a 7.3x speedup and improves hardware utilization by up to 5.6x compared to existing frameworks.

title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
summary: The authors demonstrate that an open-weight reasoning model can be trained for native robot control using reinforcement learning exclusively in simulation. The resulting system successfully transfers its learned skills to real-world hardware and novel tasks without requiring human demonstrations.
method: The authors introduce a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) to train a 27B reasoning model at scale using robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL) on simulated tasks from LIBERO and RoboDojo.

title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
summary: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies.

title: Why Skydio Built a Lopsided Drone
abstract: Skydio’s drones have always been magical. From MIT research and early prototypes to what I would argue is still the most advanced consumer drone ever made , this is a company that makes very cool stuff. Sadly, Skydio no longer makes cool stuff for consumers , instead focusing on drone platforms for public safety, inspection, and other things that, on a good day, don’t affect me personally. Even so, a new drone from Skydio is worth paying attention to, especially when it’s as weird as this one—the F10 Lightrunner is a fixed-wing camera drone designed for autonomous deployment and high-speed flight, all while looking so lopsided that it’s surprising that it can actually fly. The benefits of asymmetrical aircraft There’s a short rabbit hole you can go down if you start looking for other examples of asymmetrical aircraft. In the 1990s, legendary aircraft designer Burt Rutan and his company Scaled Composites built some decidedly odd airplanes, including the Model 202 Boomerang . But perhaps the most famous asymmetrical aircraft was the Blohm & Voss BV 141 , a World War II-era reconnaissance plane that featured an engine in the middle alongside a crew compartment alarmingly offset out onto the right wing. The unique design was intended to give the crew the best possible view for reconnaissance missions, because in a typical single-engine aircraft, the crew sits right behind the engine, limiting forward visibility. Nearly 90 years later, the Skydio F10 is applying a similar philosophy to fixed-wing reconnaissance drones, which typically track targets by flying around them in circles. “While turning at low altitudes, it becomes very hard to avoid occluding a camera with a wing or a tail,” explains Andrew Goessling , director of engineering at Skydio. “So we were analyzing a lot of these use cases, and one of our engineers just blurted out, ‘What if we put the camera on the wingtip?’ And that’s where it all started, because as long as you only turn left, a lot of these problems just go away.” Of course, putting the camera on the F10’s wingtip creates a bunch of new problems, chief among them that the aircraft is no longer balanced. Not only is the camera payload fairly heavy relative to the total mass of the drone, but its bulk also creates greater drag. This is why the seemingly straightforward solution of putting something else (like a battery) on the other wingtip to rebalance the drone isn’t practical, says Goessling. “The issue there is that the camera represents a substantial portion of the total aircraft drag, so putting something else on the other wing would cut your flight time nearly in half.” The F10’s wing-mounted camera payload necessitated asymmetrical wings and uneven motor placement. Skydio Goessling points out that there’s nothing inherently bad about an asymmetric design like the F10; it just makes the life of engineers either a little more difficult or a little more exciting, depending on your perspective. “There were really two challenges here: What is the optimal design for an aircraft with a wingtip camera, and then once you have the design, how are you going to control it?” Any fixed-wing aircraft design has to consider three factors: distribution of mass, how thrust is distributed between the motors, and how the shape and location of the wings affect the aircraft’s aerodynamics. Once Skydio decided on their requirements for the F10—including the wingtip camera, two motors to enable controllable hovering for takeoff and landing, and a high top speed and long flight time—the engineers used a modeling-and-optimization approach to explore design options. The resulting aircraft compensates for the wing-mounted camera payload by extending just that wing to provide more lift on that side, and repositioning the motors asymmetrically to balance thrust against the added drag of the camera. Maneuvering with MegaDock The MegaDock can autonomously launch, recover, and recharge up to five F10 drones using a robot arm to grab them out of the air. Skydio An added challenge was getting the F10 to launch and recover with a robot arm, using a storage, charging, and deployment system called the MegaDock. That requires the drone to transition from hover to forward flight and then back again—a particularly difficult trick for a flying wing with no tail control surfaces (movable parts of the wing used to steer the aircraft). The F10 uses model predictive control (a control technique based on a detailed physics model of the robot) to accomplish this autonomously, and a single control policy can handle the robot all the way through its entire flight envelope, from a stationary hover to its maximum flight speed of 100 miles per hour. In other words, there’s no “hover mode” or “flight mode,” so the mission planner just tells the drone where it needs to be, and the drone will know how to get itself there. In operation, Skydio’s MegaDock can handle up to five F10s, allowing for continuous flight operations with three drones while two recharge. The entire system is fully autonomous, with humans only needed for remote supervisory control, communicating with the F10 via dual 5G cellular modems. Maximum flight time is 2 hours, and the aircraft is equipped with the same kind of magical obstacle-dodging camera setup as Skydio’s quadrotor drones. If something goes seriously wrong, an integrated parachute in the F10’s butt will deploy, lowering the drone to the ground gently enough to safely fly over people. Goessling is the first to acknowledge that the F10 Lightrunner is an unconventional design, but he’s proud of what he and his team have come up with as a commercially viable solution to the occlusion issue with other fixed-wing drones. “It looks weird, and we got some pushback from some of the less technical parts of the company,” Goessling says. “If there were less crazy ways of doing it, we would have pursued them. But we have the data. We have sound reasons for every decision we’ve made. And the outcome at the end was well worth it.”
summary: IEEE Spectrum reports on Skydio's new F10 Lightrunner, an unconventional asymmetrical fixed-wing drone designed for autonomous deployment and high-speed flight. The publisher details how the aircraft features a wingtip-mounted camera and specialized controls to optimize reconnaissance missions and avoid camera occlusion.

title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
abstract: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.

title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems
abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.

title: Listening and Mirroring: The Effects of Verbal Attunement and Behavioral Mimicry on Social and Empathic Perceptions of Embodied AI Agents in VR
abstract: As embodied agents take on increasingly social and relational roles in VR, visual realism and embodiment alone may be insufficient; users must also perceive these agents as emotionally attuned, supportive, and humanlike. Prior work suggests that verbal attunement and nonverbal mimicry can each improve users’ social evaluations of embodied agents. However, behavioral mimicry has largely been studied outside of real-time, conversational AI interactions, leaving limited understanding of how users respond when an agent simultaneously generates contextually responsive dialogue and adapts its nonverbal behavior during an immersive conversation. To address this gap, we developed an embodied AI counselor that combines conversational AI with real-time facial-expression and posture mimicry, while producing either verbally attuned or neutral responses. We evaluated the system in a 2 × 2 within-subjects study with 20 participants, manipulating verbal attunement and behavioral mimicry. Results showed that verbal attunement was the most reliable driver of perceived empathy. Behavioral mimicry showed a marginal relationship with perceived humanness, while greater mimicry exposure showed preliminary, exploratory positive associations with empathy, positivity, and humanness, particularly among female participants. Together, these findings show that multimodal synchrony is not a simple additive strategy for designing empathic conversational agents in VR and underscore the need to consider how verbal and nonverbal behaviors are combined during real-time interaction.

title: PROOF: Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion
abstract: Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments. However, the reliability of such systems heavily depends on visual observations, which are inherently susceptible to occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination variations, often resulting in catastrophic locomotion failures under degraded perception conditions. In this paper, we present PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion), a perceptive locomotion framework that enables robust locomotion under severe visual disturbances. Our method adopts a two-stage teacher-student learning paradigm that explicitly models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven and proprioceptive fallback behaviors, while the student predicts exteroceptive features with uncertainty and suppresses them under out-of-distribution inputs. We evaluate our method on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a RealSense D435 depth camera in real-world settings. Under normal visual conditions, our method enables the robot to successfully perform high-dynamic parkour maneuvers, including traversing large gaps, elevated platforms, and narrow beam terrains. Under severe visual degradation, such as heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes, the robot continues to maintain stable and robust locomotion performance.
summary: Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments. title: Toward Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories through Telerobotic Interventions
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific research by integrating robotics, automated experimentation, and machine learning to execute experiments autonomously. Biology and chemistry have adopted these systems. However, increasing SDL complexity heightens susceptibility to unexpected faults in automated workflows, highlighting the need for efficient recovery mechanisms. In this study, we investigate telerobotic interventions to enhance SDL resilience against unexpected failures. We developed a teleoperation interface enabling human operators to resolve disruptions during automated tasks. The interface enables precise control of a six-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robotic arm (UR3e) using a 3D mouse (3Dconnexion SpaceMouse Pro). Two velocity-based controller strategies were evaluated: (i) a coupled mode mapping all six DOFs to the 3D mouse's central knob and (ii) a decoupled mode separating translational and rotational motions. To evaluate the framework, teleoperators intervened across three SDL fault scenarios. In the first study, comparative trials showed that the decoupled controller was associated with shorter completion times and reduced rotational motion. In a second study, teleoperators performed an aiming task with and without reference-path guidance. Users were more target-driven and risk-tolerant without guidance but showed behavioral differences under different guidance strategies. These findings suggest that controller configuration and reference-path design influence operator performance during SDL fault recovery, informing teleoperation interface optimization. This work demonstrates the potential feasibility of teleoperation as a human-in-the-loop recovery mechanism for SDL workflows, combining robotic precision with human adaptability and problem-solving. These findings also provide a foundation for future studies in shared autonomy and semi-autonomous intervention.

title: Heavy Metal Acrobatics: Learning Dynamic Control for Skid-Steer Loaders
abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that \ac{RL} in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels. This work demonstrates that \ac{RL} and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors. title: Simulation-Based Evaluation of Residual DDPG-Augmented Computed Torque Control for a Cable-Driven Lower-Limb Rehabilitation Robot Model under Disturbances and Parametric Uncertainties — MATLAB/Simulink Code and Numerical Datasets
abstract: Overview This versioned research software and numerical dataset archive accompanies the revised manuscript entitled "Simulation-Based Evaluation of Residual DDPG-Augmented Computed Torque Control for a Cable-Driven Lower-Limb Rehabilitation Robot Model under Disturbances and Parametric Uncertainties." The study investigates a hybrid control framework combining nominal Computed Torque Control (CTC) with bounded residual Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) compensation for a simulated three-degree-of-freedom cable-driven lower-limb rehabilitation robot. Repository Contents The repository provides MATLAB/Simulink implementations, the archived trained DDPG agent, surviving historical training records, numerical simulation datasets, evaluation scripts, and supporting figures. The included experiments cover: Original CTC and residual DDPG tracking performance. Multi-seed DDPG training and checkpoint evaluation. Comparative evaluations of DDPG, Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3), and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). Disturbance rejection and parametric uncertainty analyses. Tracking performance across different reference trajectories. Joint-limit compliance and safety-related trade-offs. Reward-function and hyperparameter sensitivity. Numerical cable-force allocation subject to finite force constraints and idealized actuator dynamics. Comparisons with conventional and advanced feedback-control approaches. The archive also contains the 36 numbered figures from the revised manuscript, numerical summary tables, provenance records, documented dependencies, and reproduction instructions. Reproducibility and Limitations Original research experiments and newly generated reviewer-response studies are explicitly distinguished. The original model's historical actuation-path provenance cannot be established conclusively for every archived simulation. Some historical training information and executable implementations of selected advanced feedback-controller comparisons are unavailable. The archived numerical evidence has undergone file-integrity and selected numerical consistency checks. The MATLAB/Simulink workflows were executed by the authors using the deposited repository package, and the corresponding reported numerical results were successfully reproduced in the authors' local computational environment. All reported findings concern numerical simulations. The archive does not establish hardware validation, patient-level rehabilitation efficacy, or formal physical safety guarantees. title: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents
abstract: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.

title: Adaptive dimensionality reduction for efficient deep learning on temporal video datasets
abstract: Abstract In the domain of computer vision and its related research fields, especially in temporal data handling, the analysis and processing of high dimensional data is a huge problem. Challenges in deep learning-based high dimension data processing often arise from their variable length sequences and their complex data patterns. As the use of high dimensional data continues to grow, the demand for dimension reduction of complex data is growing rapidly. Dimensionality reduction is the process of reducing a high-dimensional matrix of a dataset into a lower dimension. Standard approaches based on principal component analysis, independent component analysis and others, including simple padding and truncation, can lead to data loss or unwanted computational overhead. To address this issue, we introduce a VidSqeOpt method for dimensionality reduction based on feature extraction which exploits statistical approaches with reduced dimension and optimal length finding. Our method is validated on several benchmark datasets that are based on temporal data with complex dimensionality. Cross comparison with the baseline methods shows that our proposed approach adapts to diverse tasks, achieving up to 2.0% higher accuracy while reducing per-frame processing time by at least 23.7%, down to ≤0.45 seconds.

title: Box-conditional Hypothesis Testing for Out-of-Distribution Object Detection
abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) objects is essential for ensuring the reliability and safety of object detectors in real-world deployment. We treat the decision on a detected box as a hypothesis test with the null hypothesis that the box covers an object of an in-distribution (ID) class. The null distribution changes with the size of the box and its contact with the image border, and the detector observes both. The test can therefore rank a box only against ID boxes of the same size and border contact, which gives a distribution-free bound on the false-alarm rate for each of them and uncovers the separation that one null distribution hides. The power of the test also rests on the layer it reads. Layers built only for the ID classes have no reason to keep what sets an unknown object apart, so the test reads the features before them. We propose \textbf{PLUM}, a training-free score that pools the last backbone stage inside the box and ranks its distance to the ID classes among ID boxes of the same size and border contact. On the standard benchmark, PLUM reaches the highest AUROC among the compared methods without external models, with 91.5 and 94.5 on PASCAL-VOC and 95.1 and 97.5 on BDD100K. title: Modeling the Frictional Contact of Continuum Robots with Environments through Linear Complementarity Problem
abstract: Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism's internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots. Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications. Experimental validations demonstrated that this model is able to reduce the maximum tip position error from 45.4 mm in the frictionless model to 5.85 mm in our friction-included model with a 287.9 mm-long tendon-driven continuum robot.

title: Disturbance-Aware Informative Planning in Spatiotemporal Environments
abstract: Autonomous robots are widely used for persistent monitoring of spatiotemporal environments, where quantities of interest (QoI) change across space and time and require repeated measurements. In practice, robot motion can be affected by external disturbances that vary across the environment. When such external disturbances are not considered in trajectory optimization, it can lead to inaccurate predictions of robot motion and, consequently, the information acquired about the QoI during execution. However, estimating disturbances throughout the environment can be inefficient, as disturbances in regions with little overlap with monitoring trajectories have limited impact on monitoring performance. We therefore propose a two-stage informative planning framework for unknown, spatially varying but time-invariant disturbances, combining informed disturbance sampling with disturbance-aware trajectory optimization. First, we identify where QoI measurements are needed and generate alternative paths to these locations using the environment geometry. We then prioritize disturbance measurements based on their expected reduction of disturbance uncertainty along these paths. Second, rather than optimizing information acquisition based on nominal robot motion, we incorporate the learned disturbance belief into trajectory optimization to account for its effects on robot motion and information acquisition. Across four simulation scenarios, the proposed method reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0--52.3 percent compared with environment-wide estimation and identifies paths that appear costly under nominal dynamics but become preferable when disturbances are considered.
summary: Autonomous robots are widely used for persistent monitoring of spatiotemporal environments, where quantities of interest (QoI) change across space and time and require repeated measurements. In practice, robot motion can be affected by external disturbances that vary across the environment.

title: ARCHER: From Rationale Imitation to Executable Reasoning in Small Language Models
abstract: Small language models are attractive for local, low-cost, and privacy-sensitive deployment, but they remain unreliable on mathematical reasoning tasks that require decomposition, exact computation, tool use, and verification. We introduce \textbf{ARCHER}: \textbf{A}ction-trace \textbf{R}einforcement for \textbf{C}alculator-grounded \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{R}easoning, a two-stage framework for training small language models (SLMs) to produce executable and auditable reasoning trajectories. In the first stage, ARCHER compiles free-form chain-of-thought rationales into typed action traces containing reasoning steps, calculator calls, deterministic runtime observations, verification actions, and final answers. This shifts the supervision target from imitating explanatory text to learning a tool-grounded reasoning policy. In the second stage, ARCHER refines this policy through asymmetric hierarchical reinforcement learning, using grouped and conditionally gated trajectory rewards for answer correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. Across five standard sub-10B backbones, ARCHER improves over the strongest tool-augmented baseline by 5.51 percentage points on macro-average across benchmark accuracies, including gains of 8.95 points on MATH-500 and 5.33 and 5.34 points on AIME-2024 and AIME-2025. Evaluations on two additional reasoning-specialized 7B backbones further show that executable grounding remains beneficial after reasoning-focused reinforcement learning or distillation. These results demonstrate that executable supervision and reward-guided behavioral refinement provide a general and effective training paradigm for compact mathematical reasoners.

title: From London to Morse via Binnig, Quate, and Gerber
abstract: Summary In their landmark paper introducing the atomic force microscope [Phys. Rev. Lett. 56 , 930 (1986)], Binnig, Quate, and Gerber presciently anticipated that the technique would ultimately be capable of probing interactions running the gamut from weak van der Waals interactions to strong covalent bonding. They also highlighted that the tip‐sample forces central to AFM are present, and often highly influential, in scanning tunnelling microscopy; indeed, this realisation directly inspired the invention of the force microscope. In this perspective for the Forty Years of AFM special issue, we review selected aspects of two decades of work from our group at the University of Nottingham that span the force range highlighted by BQG and are united by a common, central theme: the probe as active participant rather than passive observer. Our selection of results also covers length and correlation scales from the microscopic right down to the single chemical bond limit, tracking a spectrum of interactions from van der Waals/Hamaker forces, through hydrogen bonding, to covalent bonds and, finally, atom‐by‐atom assembly of metal clusters via vertical tip‐sample transfer. Echoing BQG's own observations on the prevalence of probe‐sample forces in STM, we also discuss recent evidence that tip‐induced heterogeneity underpins first‐passage dynamics in molecular diffusion and highlight the challenges in acquiring non‐invasive measurements of diffusion barriers for adsorbed molecules that are readily perturbed by the probe. We close with a perspective on machine learning's growing role in automating tip‐driven atomic and molecular manipulation.

title: Deep learning analysis of echo signals from a single piezoelectric element for breast mass detection: a proof-of-concept study
abstract: A palpable mass is a common presenting symptom of breast cancer, but neither breast self examination nor clinical breast examination is sensitive enough to detect breast masses early. We hypothesized that deep learning analysis of signals from a single-element (A-mode) ultrasound sensor can differentiate breast regions containing a mass from normal breast tissue. A-mode signals were prospectively acquired from 200 patients (192 malignant and 8 benign or borderline lesions). Signals collected during a freehand sweep were stacked into two-dimensional images (reconstructed A-mode images), whose appearance varies with probe motion. Self-supervised pre-training on public B-mode images was compared with ImageNet initialization, and an acquisition-specific augmentation (Variable Speed and Pressure Augmentation, VSPA) with conventional augmentation. The first 131 patients were used for model development and the next 69 for additional validation. On additional validation, ultrasound pre-training gave higher region-level AUCs than ImageNet initialization (ResNet-50, 93.6% versus 91.7%; ViT-B/16, 96.3% versus 93.2%) and more mass-focused Grad-CAM heatmaps. For ViT-B/16, the advantage grew as training data decreased. Conventional spatial augmentation gave most of the gain (ViT-B/16, 96.8% versus 93.2%), and VSPA added little. Further validation in women without known breast lesions is needed before this approach can be considered for screening.

title: Discrimination of ranges of closely related RNA targets using CRISPR-based detection assay developed using machine learning-based optimization
abstract: Abstract Early detection and identification of pathogen strains are crucial for mitigating infectious disease threats, including those posed by closely related zoonotic variants. A key limitation of current molecular detection approaches is their narrow focus on individual targets, which can delay recognition of outbreaks caused by closely related but non-identical pathogens. Here we report a two-channel CRISPR/Cas13a detection assay capable of discriminating between SARS-CoV-2 and a panel of twelve closely related zoonotic sarbecoviruses using a compact duplex assay format. Guide RNA sets with tunable specificity were designed using a two-stage machine learning pipeline: initial candidate filtering with a pre-existing RuleFit model, followed by retraining on 382 sarbecovirus-specific in vitro data points to refine the mismatch threshold from 4 to 6 mismatches for target exclusion. The optimized assay achieved proof-of-concept three-way classification of synthetic RNA targets into: (1) SARS-CoV-2, (2) the closest known near-neighbor BANAL-236, and (3) remaining zoonotic near-neighbors, with a limit of detection of 15–150 fM for synthetic RNA targets. This approach provides a practical framework for surveillance-oriented detection that identifies not only a specific pathogen but also its closest relatives, provided that system-specific validation and model retraining are included for new target systems.

title: Multimodal Haptic Display Integrating Texture, Softness, and Thermal Rendering for Active Touch
abstract: ABSTRACT Touch allows humans to perceive fundamental cues, such as roughness, friction, softness, and temperature, that define how surfaces feel. Yet these sensations remain largely absent from digital interactions. Here, we present SensaSurf, a unified haptic display that delivers the four primary tactile modalities during active fingertip exploration. SensaSurf combines electrovibration for roughness and friction, a pneumatically actuated origami joint for stiffness, and a temperature‐controlled origami bellows for thermal and contact area modulation, enabling independent control of lateral force, effective stiffness, contact area, and temperature across perceptually relevant ranges. A user study showed that these capabilities produce distinct multimodal sensations spanning major dimensions of touch. To our knowledge, SensaSurf is the first surface‐based haptic display to integrate all primary tactile modalities during active bare‐finger interaction, opening opportunities to study multisensory perception and to advance multimodal tactile surface rendering in digital environments.

title: JVT: Just Video Transformer makes pixel-space video diffusion simple
abstract: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.

title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors
abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}γ\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.
summary: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures
abstract: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.

title: CoPre-MoE: Consolidating and Preserving MoE for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
abstract: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.
summary: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination.

title: Structural Self-Teaching for Compositional Generation in Unified Multimodal Models
abstract: We propose Structural Self-Teaching (SST), a novel framework that enhances compositional image generation in diffusion-based unified multimodal models (UMMs) by leveraging their internal understanding path as a source of structural supervision. The generation path of UMMs often struggles with dense compositional prompts, leading to missing objects, attribute binding failures, and spatial errors. In contrast, their understanding path localizes the same phrases in images that satisfy these prompts. SST converts this phrase-level grounding into training-time structural signals for the generation path. Specifically, we extract phrase-conditioned support masks from internal attention maps derived from the understanding path and employ them through two mechanisms. Phrase-local contrastive alignment uses these masks as pooling regions and aligns each generated phrase region with the same region of the target image. A structural scaffold builds a phrase-level layout from the same masks and modulates an intermediate spatial state of the generation path during training. The scaffold is phased out during training and removed at inference. SST requires no external structural annotations for training and no additional input at test time. Extensive experiments across multiple UMMs demonstrate that SST improves compositional fidelity over LoRA fine-tuning on the same data, with no inference-time cost. Project page is available at https://bellos1203.github.io/sst

title: NPU-Accelerated GNSS Signal Acquisition
abstract: On small single-board computers (SBCs), GNSS signal acquisition is a major CPU load. This paper proposes using the neural processing unit (NPU) of an SBC not for machine learning but as an accelerator for the parallel code search in GNSS signal acquisition. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) used in acquisition is decomposed by the four-step DFT into matrix products of small DFTs and expressed by $1\times1$ convolutions, element-wise products, and transposes, which NPUs execute efficiently. Furthermore, we propose a method that divides the DFT, the non-coherent integration, and the peak detection between the CPU and the NPU according to the configuration of the NPU (an NPU with its own memory connected via PCIe, or an NPU sharing memory with the CPU). The proposed method is implemented in the open-source software GNSS receiver Pocket SDR and evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 5 combined with the external AX8850 NPU and on the NPU built into the SoC (RK3588) of the ROCK 5C, a small SBC of comparable size. Compared with acquisition by an optimized CPU implementation, the acquisition of short codes on the Raspberry Pi 5 with the AX8850 is 3.0-3.8 times faster. In the evaluation of the whole receiver, the number of tracking channels that reach their first lock within 30 s with the NPU is 1.5 times that with the CPU, and the time until 90% of the channels are locked is reduced from 66 s to 26 s. Furthermore, because the CPU load of acquisition is reduced, the number of tracking channels that can be processed in real time increases from about 175 to about 230. These results show that using the NPU on SBCs with limited CPU resources is effective for achieving both GNSS signal acquisition and tracking. The implementation is publicly available as open source under the name PocketSDR-NPU.
